excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework is a set of protocols that aims to address severe risks that may arise from the high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.
paraphrase: The Framework consists of protocols designed to address severe risks from frontier AI models' high-impact capabilities.

excerpt: It complements Google's suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, and enables AI innovation and deployment consistent with our AI Principles.
paraphrase: The Framework works alongside Google's other safety practices and supports AI innovation consistent with its AI Principles.

excerpt: The Framework is informed by the broader conversation on Frontier AI Safety and Security Frameworks.
paraphrase: The Framework draws on wider discourse regarding Frontier AI Safety and Security Frameworks.

excerpt: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
paraphrase: The document introduces a list of core components shared by such frameworks.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Identify capability levels at which frontier AI models, without additional mitigations, could pose severe risk.
paraphrase: One core component is identifying capability levels that could pose severe risk absent mitigations.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Implement protocols to detect the attainment of such capability levels throughout the model lifecycle.
paraphrase: Another component is implementing detection protocols across the model's lifecycle.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Prepare and articulate proactive mitigation plans to ensure severe risks are adequately mitigated when such capability levels are attained.
paraphrase: Another component is preparing proactive mitigation plans for when capability levels are reached.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Where required or appropriate, involve external parties to help inform and guide the approach.
paraphrase: The final component is involving external parties when required or appropriate to guide the approach.

excerpt: In the Framework, we specify protocols for the detection of capability levels at which frontier AI models may pose severe risks (which we call "Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)"), and articulate mitigation approaches to address such risks.
paraphrase: The Framework specifies detection protocols for Critical Capability Levels and articulates mitigation approaches.

excerpt: The Framework addresses misuse risk, risks from machine learning research and development (ML R&D), and misalignment risk.
paraphrase: The Framework covers three risk categories: misuse, ML R&D, and misalignment.

excerpt: For each type of risk, we define a set of CCLs and a mitigation approach for them.
paraphrase: Each risk type has an associated set of CCLs and mitigation approach.

excerpt: Risk assessment will necessarily involve evaluating cross-cutting capabilities such as agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.
paraphrase: Risk assessment must evaluate cross-cutting capabilities including agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.

excerpt: The safety and security of frontier AI models is a global public good.
paraphrase: Frontier AI model safety and security are framed as a global public good.

excerpt: The protocols here represent our current understanding and approach of how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
paraphrase: The protocols reflect the current understanding and approach to anticipating and addressing severe frontier AI risks.

excerpt: Importantly, there are certain mitigations whose social value is significantly reduced if not broadly applied to frontier AI models reaching critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Some mitigations lose much of their social value unless broadly adopted across frontier AI models reaching critical capabilities.

excerpt: These mitigations are most effective when adopted by industry as a whole: our adoption of them would result in effective risk mitigation for society only if all relevant organisations provide similar levels of protection.
paraphrase: Such mitigations work best industry-wide; unilateral adoption alone would not produce effective societal risk mitigation.

excerpt: The Framework is based on early and evolving research.
paraphrase: The Framework rests on research that is still early-stage and evolving.

excerpt: We may change our approach over time as we gain experience and insights on the projected capabilities of future frontier models.
paraphrase: The approach may change as more experience and insight is gained about future frontier model capabilities.

excerpt: We will review the Framework periodically and we expect it to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves.
paraphrase: The Framework will be reviewed periodically and is expected to evolve substantially as understanding improves.

excerpt: See https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/emerging-processes-for-frontier-ai-safety, https://metr.org/faisc, https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropics-responsible-scaling-policy, https://openai.com/index/updating-our-preparedness-framework/, https://www.frontiermodelforum.org/publications/#technical-reports.
paraphrase: The footnote lists external references on frontier AI safety frameworks from other organizations.

excerpt: As in, in the context of the Framework, risks of threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.
paraphrase: Misuse risk refers to threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.

excerpt: Misalignment can pose a number of risks. In the context of the Framework, we address specific scenarios where general-purpose AI agents are potentially misaligned and can become difficult to control, thereby posing a risk of severe harm.
paraphrase: The footnote clarifies that misalignment risk here refers to scenarios where general-purpose AI agents become misaligned and hard to control, posing severe harm risk.

excerpt: This section describes the central components of the Frontier Safety Framework.
paraphrase: This section introduces the central components of the Framework.

excerpt: These protocols represent our current understanding of and approach for how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
paraphrase: The protocols reflect the current understanding of and approach to anticipating and addressing severe frontier AI risks.

excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework focuses on possible severe risks stemming from high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.
paraphrase: The Framework's focus is severe risks that may stem from high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.

excerpt: The Framework complements Google's suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, which address other risks in addition to the severe risks in scope of the Framework in accordance with our AI Principles.
paraphrase: The Framework complements Google's broader AI responsibility and safety practices that also address other risks beyond the Framework's scope.

excerpt: The approaches and mitigations outlined in the Framework are not exclusive to models where we believe a severe risk could arise and are part of Google's comprehensive AI responsibility and safety practices.
paraphrase: The Framework's approaches and mitigations are not limited to models believed to pose severe risk, and form part of Google's wider AI responsibility practices.

excerpt: The Framework is built around capability thresholds called "Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)."
paraphrase: The Framework's central structure consists of capability thresholds termed Critical Capability Levels.

excerpt: These are capability levels at which, absent mitigation measures, frontier AI models or systems may pose heightened risk of severe harm.
paraphrase: CCLs are levels where, without mitigations, models may pose heightened severe harm risk.

excerpt: CCLs are determined by identifying and analyzing the main foreseeable paths through which a model could result in severe harm: we then define the CCLs as the minimal set of capabilities a model must possess to do so.
paraphrase: CCLs are set by analyzing foreseeable paths to severe harm and defining the minimal capability set needed for such harm.

excerpt: We describe three sets of CCLs: misuse CCLs, machine learning R&D CCLs, and misalignment CCLs.
paraphrase: There are three categories of CCLs: misuse, ML R&D, and misalignment.

excerpt: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
paraphrase: The document introduces the misuse risk domains for which CCLs are defined.

context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
excerpt: CBRN: Risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear ("CBRN") threat.
paraphrase: CBRN risk domain covers models assisting in creating or executing chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear threats.

context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
excerpt: Cyber: Risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a cyber attack.
paraphrase: Cyber risk domain covers models assisting in developing or executing cyber attacks.

context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
excerpt: Harmful Manipulation: Risks of models with high manipulative capabilities potentially being misused in ways that could reasonably result in large scale harm.
paraphrase: Harmful Manipulation covers risks from highly manipulative model capabilities being misused to cause large-scale harm.

excerpt: For machine learning R&D risk, we define CCLs that identify when ML R&D capabilities in our models may, if not properly managed, reduce society's overall ability to manage AI risks.
paraphrase: ML R&D CCLs identify when ML R&D capabilities, if mismanaged, could reduce society's ability to manage AI risks.

excerpt: Such capabilities may serve as a substantial cross-cutting risk factor for other pathways to severe harm.
paraphrase: ML R&D capabilities may act as a substantial cross-cutting factor contributing to other severe harm pathways.

excerpt: For misalignment risk, we outline an exploratory approach that focuses on detecting when models might develop a baseline instrumental reasoning ability at which they have the potential to undermine human control, assuming no additional mitigations were applied.
paraphrase: For misalignment risk, an exploratory approach detects when models might reach baseline instrumental reasoning ability enabling them to undermine human control absent mitigations.

excerpt: Most CCLs define one important component of our risk acceptance criteria.
paraphrase: Most CCLs form one key part of the risk acceptance criteria.

excerpt: Because the CCLs for misalignment risk are exploratory and intended for illustration only, we do not associate them with explicit risk acceptance criteria.
paraphrase: Misalignment CCLs are exploratory/illustrative only and thus lack explicit risk acceptance criteria.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: For each risk domain, we conduct aspects of our risk assessment at various moments throughout the model development process, both before and after deployment.
paraphrase: Risk assessment for each domain occurs at multiple points across model development, before and after deployment.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: We conduct a risk assessment for the first external deployment of a new frontier AI model.
paraphrase: A risk assessment is conducted for a new frontier model's first external deployment.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: For subsequent versions of the model, we conduct a further risk assessment if the model has meaningful new capabilities or a material increase in performance, until the model is retired or we deploy a more capable model.
paraphrase: For later model versions, further risk assessments occur when meaningful new capabilities or material performance increases arise, continuing until retirement or replacement by a more capable model.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: The reason for this is because a material change in the model's capabilities may mean that the risk profile of the model has changed or the justification for why the risks stemming from the model are acceptable has been materially undermined.
paraphrase: This is because material capability changes may alter the risk profile or undermine the original justification for acceptable risk.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: To identify meaningful new capabilities or material increases in performance, we conduct model capability evaluations, including our automated benchmarks.
paraphrase: Model capability evaluations, including automated benchmarks, are used to identify meaningful new capabilities or performance increases.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: These evaluations are primarily aimed at understanding the capabilities of the model and may be triggered, for example, upon the completion of a pre-training or post-training run, on various candidates of a model version.
paraphrase: These evaluations aim to understand model capabilities and may be triggered by completion of training runs on various model candidates.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: These evaluations include a broad range of areas, including general capability evaluations, model behavior, efficiency, coding capabilities, multilinguality, or reasoning.
paraphrase: The evaluations span general capability, model behavior, efficiency, coding, multilinguality, and reasoning.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: Data from these evaluations are collected and analyzed to give us an indication as to how the model is performing and whether a risk assessment is necessary.
paraphrase: Evaluation data is collected and analyzed to indicate model performance and whether a risk assessment is needed.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps (which do not need to be repeated where a previous risk assessment is still appropriate):
paraphrase: The risk assessment process involves listed steps, which need not be repeated if a prior assessment remains valid.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps: Identification —
excerpt: As explained above, we have identified risk domains where, based on early research, we have determined severe risks may be most likely to arise from future models: CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, and machine learning R&D.
paraphrase: Identification involves the risk domains determined via early research as most likely for severe risk: CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, and ML R&D.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps: Identification —
excerpt: As part of our broader research into frontier AI models, we continue to assess whether there are other risk domains where severe risks may arise and will update our approach as appropriate.
paraphrase: Broader research continues to assess whether additional risk domains exist, with the approach updated as appropriate.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps: Identification —
excerpt: For each of the four identified domains, we have developed specific scenarios in which these risks could materialize.
paraphrase: Specific scenarios have been developed for each of the four identified risk domains.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps: Analysis —
excerpt: Central to our model evaluations are "early warning evaluations," to assess the proximity of the model to a CCL.
paraphrase: Early warning evaluations assess how close a model is to reaching a CCL.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps: Analysis —
excerpt: We define "alert thresholds" for these evaluations that are designed to flag when a CCL may be reached before a risk assessment is conducted again.
paraphrase: Alert thresholds are defined to flag potential approach of a CCL before the next risk assessment.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps: Analysis —
excerpt: In our evaluations, we seek to equip the model with appropriate scaffolding and other augmentations to make it more likely that we are also assessing the capabilities of systems that will likely be produced with the model.
paraphrase: Evaluations aim to include scaffolding and augmentations to better reflect capabilities of systems likely to be built with the model.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps: Analysis —
excerpt: We may run early warning evaluations more frequently or adjust the alert threshold of our evaluations if the rate of progress suggests our safety buffer is no longer adequate.
paraphrase: Evaluation frequency or alert thresholds may be adjusted if progress suggests the safety buffer is inadequate.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps: Analysis —
excerpt: We conduct further analysis, including reviewing model independent information, external evaluations, and post-market monitoring as appropriate.
paraphrase: Further analysis includes model-independent information review, external evaluations, and post-market monitoring as appropriate.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps: Acceptance determination and mitigations —
excerpt: We then determine whether the model has met or will meet a CCL and, if so, whether we need to implement any further mitigations to reduce the risk to an acceptable level (see below).
paraphrase: The final step determines whether a CCL has been or will be met, and whether further mitigations are needed to reduce risk to acceptable level.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: Our approach to model evaluations and risk assessments described above means we can proactively monitor a model's capabilities throughout the entire lifecycle of the model and ensure that any severe risk is properly identified and mitigated.
paraphrase: This approach enables proactive monitoring of model capabilities across the whole lifecycle, ensuring proper identification and mitigation of severe risk.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: Where appropriate, we may engage relevant and appropriate external actors, including governments, to inform our responsible development and deployment practices.
paraphrase: External actors, including governments, may be engaged where appropriate to inform responsible development and deployment practices.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
locator: Note on Machine Learning R&D CCLs
excerpt: Risk assessment must take into account the fact that other actors may put significantly more effort into eliciting capabilities than we put into assessing risk, thus requiring conservatism in the form of evaluations.
paraphrase: Risk assessment must account for the possibility that other actors invest more in eliciting capabilities than the assessing organization does, requiring conservative evaluations.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
locator: Note on Machine Learning R&D CCLs
excerpt: However, as a frontier AI company, we do not expect other groups to put significantly more effort into ML R&D than we do ourselves.
paraphrase: As a frontier AI company, the organization does not expect other groups to invest more into ML R&D than it does.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
locator: Note on Machine Learning R&D CCLs
excerpt: As a result, to assess the ML R&D CCLs, we may use sources of information about our own progress at accelerating ML R&D to assess whether we are near or at the CCLs, in addition to evaluations of ML R&D capabilities.
paraphrase: ML R&D CCL assessment may draw on information about internal progress accelerating ML R&D, alongside capability evaluations.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
locator: Note on Machine Learning R&D CCLs
excerpt: Similarly, our alert threshold may be defined based on these sources of information, rather than on evaluation scores.
paraphrase: Alert thresholds may likewise rely on these internal information sources rather than evaluation scores.

section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
excerpt: We exclude misalignment risk from this list of domains because of its exploratory nature.
paraphrase: Misalignment risk is excluded from the domain list due to its exploratory nature.

excerpt: We apply safety and security mitigations throughout the lifecycle of our models, including as part of our training and model development phase and, where appropriate, before CCLs are reached as described in the process below.
paraphrase: Safety and security mitigations are applied throughout the model lifecycle, including during training/development and, where appropriate, before CCLs are reached.

excerpt: When a model reaches an alert threshold for a CCL, we will assess the proximity of the model to the CCL and analyze the risk posed, involving internal and external experts as needed.
paraphrase: When a model reaches an alert threshold, proximity to the CCL and risk posed will be assessed, involving internal and external experts as needed.

excerpt: This will inform the formulation and application of a response plan.
paraphrase: The assessment informs the response plan's formulation and application.

excerpt: Where model capabilities remain quite distant from a CCL, a response plan may involve the adoption of additional capability assessment processes to flag when heightened mitigations are required.
paraphrase: If a model is far from a CCL, the response plan may add capability assessment processes to flag when stronger mitigations become needed.

excerpt: Central to most response plans will be the application of the mitigations described later in this document.
paraphrase: Most response plans center on the mitigations described later in the document.

excerpt: We have two categories of mitigations: security mitigations (such as preventing the exfiltration of model weights), and deployment mitigations (such as safety fine-tuning and monitoring and response) intended to counter the misuse or misaligned expression of critical capabilities in deployments.
paraphrase: There are two mitigation categories: security mitigations (e.g., preventing weight exfiltration) and deployment mitigations (e.g., safety fine-tuning, monitoring) aimed at countering misuse or misaligned expression of critical capabilities.

excerpt: Note that these mitigations reflect considerations from the perspective of addressing severe risks from powerful capabilities alone; due to this focused scope, other risk management and security considerations may result in more stringent mitigations applied to a model than specified by the Framework.
paraphrase: These mitigations only address severe risk from powerful capabilities; other considerations may lead to stricter mitigations than the Framework specifies.

excerpt: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
paraphrase: Various processes will assess mitigation effectiveness and limitations.

context_stem: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
excerpt: Security mitigations: security infrastructure at Google is subject to penetration testing and other kinds of assessments, and is continually improved based on these results.
paraphrase: Security mitigations are evaluated through penetration testing and other assessments and continually improved.

context_stem: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
excerpt: Deployment mitigations: we will use a combination of threat modeling, empirical testing, and other sources of information to assess the effectiveness and limitations of our deployment mitigations.
paraphrase: Deployment mitigations are assessed via threat modeling, empirical testing, and other information sources.

context_stem: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
excerpt: These will form the basis of a safety case for models reaching CCLs, that will be reviewed before deployment.
paraphrase: These assessments form the safety case for models reaching CCLs, reviewed before deployment.

context_stem: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
excerpt: See the deployment mitigations sections below for misuse and machine learning R&D for more.
paraphrase: Further detail on deployment mitigations appears in later sections on misuse and ML R&D.

excerpt: The Framework outlines a variety of risk acceptance criteria for different model risks and capabilities pertaining to severe risks.
paraphrase: The Framework sets out varied risk acceptance criteria across different model risks and capabilities.

excerpt: A model for which risk assessment indicates no CCL is reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of severe risk for further development and deployment, because it should not possess the capabilities required to substantially contribute to severe risk scenarios.
paraphrase: If no CCL is reached, the model is deemed acceptable risk for development and deployment since it lacks capabilities substantially contributing to severe risk.

excerpt: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a misuse CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
paraphrase: If a misuse CCL is reached, the model may still be deemed acceptable risk under certain example conditions.

context_stem: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a misuse CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
excerpt: We assess that the deployment mitigations have brought the risk of severe harm to an appropriate level proportionate to the risk, based on considerations such as whether the risk has been reduced to an acceptable level by mitigations, the scope of the deployment, what capabilities and mitigations are available on other publicly available models (e.g. if other models are similarly capable and have few mitigations, then the marginal risk added by our release is likely low), and the historical incidence and severity of related events.
paraphrase: Acceptability is assessed based on whether mitigations reduce risk proportionately, considering deployment scope, comparable models' mitigations, and historical incidence/severity of related events.

context_stem: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a misuse CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
excerpt: This is required only for external deployment, not further development.
paraphrase: This assessment requirement applies only to external deployment, not to further development.

context_stem: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a misuse CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
excerpt: Security mitigations have been applied to the model weights reaching the recommended security level stated below, or we otherwise assess that the level of security applied is adequate, e.g. if they match or exceed the level of security applied to other models with similar capabilities or risk profiles, or we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
paraphrase: Acceptability also depends on applying the recommended security level to model weights, or otherwise assessing security as adequate relative to comparable models, or judging that open release benefits outweigh risks.

excerpt: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a machine learning R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
paraphrase: If an ML R&D CCL is reached, the model may still be deemed acceptable risk under certain example conditions.

context_stem: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a machine learning R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
excerpt: We assess that the deployment mitigations have brought the risk of severe harm to an appropriate level proportionate to the risk, based on considerations such as whether the risk has been reduced to an acceptable level by mitigations, and information pertaining to model propensities and the severity of related events.
paraphrase: Acceptability depends on mitigations proportionately reducing risk, considering model propensities and severity of related events.

context_stem: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a machine learning R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
excerpt: This is required only for external deployment and large scale internal deployment, not further development.
paraphrase: This requirement applies to external deployment and large-scale internal deployment only, not to further development.

context_stem: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a machine learning R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
excerpt: Security mitigations have been applied to the model weights reaching the recommended security level stated below, or we otherwise assess that the level of security applied is adequate, e.g. if they match or exceed the level of security applied to other models with similar capabilities or risk profiles, or we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
paraphrase: Acceptability also depends on applying recommended security levels, or otherwise assessing security adequacy relative to comparable models, or judging open release benefits outweigh risks.

excerpt: Because the CCLs for misalignment risk are exploratory and intended for illustration only, we do not associate them with explicit risk acceptance criteria.
paraphrase: Misalignment CCLs, being exploratory/illustrative, lack explicit risk acceptance criteria.

excerpt: Assessing frontier AI capabilities and corresponding severe risk is a complex process.
paraphrase: Assessing frontier AI capabilities and corresponding severe risk is complex.

excerpt: Because the science of AI risk assessment is still developing, our assessments will often involve some level of subjective analysis.
paraphrase: Since AI risk assessment science is still developing, assessments often involve subjective analysis.

excerpt: The concept of proportionality is central to our determination of whether a particular mitigation has sufficiently reduced the risk to acceptable levels.
paraphrase: Proportionality is central to determining whether a mitigation has sufficiently reduced risk to acceptable levels.

excerpt: The mitigation and the effects of such mitigation should also be assessed holistically and be commensurate with expected impact of a model's risk, thus balancing safety with innovation.
paraphrase: Mitigations and their effects should be assessed holistically, proportionate to the model's expected risk impact, balancing safety and innovation.

excerpt: A safety case is an assessable argument showing how severe risks associated with a model's CCLs have been reduced to an appropriate level. See also, for reference, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01420.
paraphrase: A safety case is defined as an assessable argument showing severe risks from a model's CCLs have been reduced to an appropriate level.

excerpt: Note that this does not mean that no mitigations will be implemented prior to the deployment of the model. We apply safety and security mitigations throughout the lifecycle of our models for a whole host of potential risks, including as part of our training and model development phase.
paraphrase: The footnote clarifies that mitigations are still applied prior to deployment across the model lifecycle for many potential risks, including during training and development.

excerpt: This section is limited to those mitigations that will be required to bring a model to an acceptable level of risk relative just to the specific CCL, which by definition pose the greatest risks of severe harm.
paraphrase: This section covers only the mitigations required to bring risk to acceptable levels for the specific CCL, which by definition pose the greatest severe harm risk.

excerpt: Note that deployment mitigations for the ML R&D CCLs are different than those for the misuse CCLs because of differences in which deployment could lead to severe harm for those respective categories.
paraphrase: Deployment mitigations differ between ML R&D and misuse CCLs due to differing pathways to severe harm in deployment.

excerpt: In contrast, security mitigations protecting against weights exfiltration are generally beneficial to both kinds of risk.
paraphrase: Security mitigations against weights exfiltration generally benefit both misuse and ML R&D risk categories.

excerpt: This section describes our mitigation approach for models that pose risks of severe harm through misuse, and then details our set of misuse CCLs (CBRN, cyber and harmful manipulation), as well as the mitigation approach that we assess as appropriate for them.
paraphrase: This section covers the mitigation approach for misuse-related severe harm and details the misuse CCLs and their corresponding mitigation approaches.

excerpt: There are two categories of mitigations to address models with misuse critical capabilities: security mitigations intended to prevent the exfiltration of model weights, and deployment mitigations intended to counter the misuse of critical capabilities in external deployments.
paraphrase: Two mitigation categories address misuse critical capabilities: security mitigations preventing weight exfiltration, and deployment mitigations countering misuse in external deployments.

excerpt: For security, we have several levels of mitigations, allowing calibration of the appropriateness and robustness of security measures to the risks posed.
paraphrase: Multiple security mitigation levels allow calibrating measure robustness to the risk posed.

excerpt: For deployment mitigations, we specify a standard process for applying, assessing, and reviewing mitigations: the aim of this process is to calibrate mitigations to CCLs, and the procedural approach reflects the more iterative and CCL-dependent nature of deployment mitigations.
paraphrase: A standard process governs applying, assessing, and reviewing deployment mitigations, calibrated to CCLs and reflecting their iterative, CCL-dependent nature.

excerpt: This structured process for deployment mitigations is centered on assessing and reviewing that the risk of severe harm has been brought to an appropriate level proportionate to the risk.
paraphrase: The deployment mitigation process centers on assessing/reviewing that severe harm risk has been reduced proportionately.

excerpt: Security mitigations against exfiltration risk, such as identity and access management practices and hardening interface-access to unreleased model parameters, are important for models reaching CCLs.
paraphrase: Security mitigations like identity/access management and hardened interface access are important for models reaching CCLs.

excerpt: This is because the release of model weights may enable the removal of any safeguards trained into or deployed with the model, and hence access (including by threat actors) to any critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Weight release may allow removal of trained/deployed safeguards, enabling access to critical capabilities including by threat actors.

excerpt: Here, we use security levels that indicate goals/principles in line with the corresponding level in the RAND framework.
paraphrase: Security levels used here align with goals/principles at corresponding levels in the RAND framework.

excerpt: Because AI security is an area of active research, we expect the concrete measures implemented to reach each level of security to evolve substantially.
paraphrase: Since AI security research is active, concrete measures for reaching security levels are expected to evolve substantially.

excerpt: In other words, "security level N" indicates security controls and detections at a level generally aligned with RAND SL N.
paraphrase: Security level N corresponds generally to RAND SL N security controls and detections.

excerpt: See https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2849-1.html, pp 21-22. In aligning our security levels with RAND's, we are referring to the security goals and principles in the RAND framework, rather than the benchmarks (i.e. concrete measures) also described in the RAND report.
paraphrase: Alignment with RAND refers to security goals/principles, not the concrete benchmark measures also in the RAND report.

excerpt: As the authors point out, the "security level benchmarks represent neither a complete standard nor a compliance regime—they are provided for informational purposes only and should inform security teams' decisions rather than supersede them."
paraphrase: RAND's authors state security level benchmarks are informational only, meant to inform rather than replace security team decisions.

excerpt: The following mitigation process for external deployments will be applied to models reaching a misuse CCL, allowing for iterative and flexible tailoring of mitigations to each risk and use case.
paraphrase: A defined mitigation process for external deployments applies to models reaching a misuse CCL, tailored iteratively per risk and use case.

excerpt: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
paraphrase: Step 1 covers developing safeguards and a safety case through iteration.

context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
excerpt: Developing and improving a suite of safeguards targeting the capability, which may include measures such as safety post-training, monitoring and analysis, account moderation, jailbreak detection and patching, user verification, and bug bounties.
paraphrase: Sub-step (a) involves developing/improving safeguards such as safety post-training, monitoring, account moderation, jailbreak detection, user verification, and bug bounties.

context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
excerpt: Assessing the robustness of these mitigations against the risk posed through testing (e.g. automated evaluations, red teaming) and threat modeling research.
paraphrase: Sub-step (b) involves assessing mitigation robustness through testing methods and threat modeling research.

context_stem: Assessing the robustness of these mitigations against the risk posed through testing and threat modeling research.
excerpt: The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
paraphrase: The assessment is structured as a safety case that may consider several listed factors.

context_stem: The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: How much the risk has been reduced by mitigations. For example, whether tests run on mitigated models suggest that the refusal rate and jailbreak robustness together imply the risk has been brought substantially lower than that posed by a model reaching the CCL without mitigations.
paraphrase: One factor is the extent of risk reduction from mitigations, e.g. whether refusal rate and jailbreak robustness testing indicate substantially lower risk than an unmitigated CCL-reaching model.

context_stem: The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: The likelihood and consequences of model misuse, capability improvements after the risk assessment, and likelihood and consequences of our mitigations being circumvented, deactivated, or subverted.
paraphrase: Another factor is the likelihood/consequences of misuse, post-assessment capability improvements, and mitigation circumvention risks.

context_stem: The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: The scope of the deployment. For example, small scale and private deployments may pose substantially less risk than large scale or public deployments.
paraphrase: Another factor is deployment scope, with small/private deployments posing less risk than large-scale/public ones.

context_stem: The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: What capabilities and mitigations are available on other publicly available models. For example, whether another (non-Google) publicly deployed model is at the same CCL, and has mitigations that are less effective at preventing misuse than that of the model being assessed, in which case the deployment of this model is less likely to materially increase risk.
paraphrase: Another factor is comparison to other publicly available models' capabilities and mitigations; weaker mitigations elsewhere at the same CCL suggest the assessed model's deployment adds less marginal risk.

context_stem: The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: The historical incidence and severity of related events: for example, whether data suggests a high (or low) likelihood of attempted misuse of models at the CCL.
paraphrase: Another factor is historical incidence/severity of related events, such as data on likelihood of attempted misuse at the CCL.

context_stem: The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
excerpt: Mitigations would consequently have to be stronger (or would not have to be so strong) for deployment to be appropriate.
paraphrase: Mitigation strength requirements scale with the historical incidence/severity data for deployment to be appropriate.

excerpt: Pre-deployment review of safety case: external deployments of a model take place only after the appropriate governance function determines the safety case regarding each CCL the model has reached to be adequate.
paraphrase: Step 2 requires that external deployment occur only after the governance function deems the safety case adequate for each reached CCL.

excerpt: In particular, we will deem deployment mitigations adequate if the evidence suggests that for the CCLs the model has reached, the increase in likelihood of severe harm has been reduced to an acceptable level.
paraphrase: Deployment mitigations are deemed adequate if evidence shows the increased likelihood of severe harm from reached CCLs has been reduced to an acceptable level.

excerpt: Post-deployment processes: our safety cases and mitigations may be updated if deemed necessary by post-market monitoring.
paraphrase: Step 3 allows updating safety cases and mitigations post-deployment if post-market monitoring deems it necessary.

excerpt: Material updates to a safety case will be submitted to the appropriate governance function for review.
paraphrase: Material safety case updates must be submitted to the governance function for review.

excerpt: This process is designed to ensure that residual risk remains at acceptable levels: evidence of efficacy collected during development and testing, as well as expert-driven estimates of other parameters, will enable us to assess residual risk and to detect substantial changes that invalidate our risk assessment.
paraphrase: The process aims to keep residual risk acceptable, using development/testing efficacy evidence and expert estimates to assess residual risk and detect invalidating changes.

excerpt: With iteration on safeguards and safety cases, we believe that we are able to make informed decisions about the level of risk via a CCL before a model is released, and reliably prevent models posing unacceptable levels of risk from being deployed.
paraphrase: Iterative safeguards and safety cases are believed to enable informed pre-release risk decisions and reliably prevent deployment of unacceptably risky models.

excerpt: The table below details a set of CCLs we have identified through ongoing analysis of the CBRN, cyber, and harmful manipulation risk domains.
paraphrase: The table lists CCLs identified through ongoing analysis of CBRN, cyber, and harmful manipulation domains.

excerpt: We expect these to evolve over time.
paraphrase: The CCLs are expected to change over time.

excerpt: We recommend a security level for each of these CCLs, which reflect our assessment of the minimum appropriate level of security the field of frontier AI should apply to models reaching each CCL.
paraphrase: A recommended security level accompanies each CCL, reflecting the assessed minimum appropriate security the frontier AI field should apply.

excerpt: In practice, our overall security posture may commonly exceed the baseline levels recommended here.
paraphrase: Actual security posture may often exceed the recommended baseline levels.

excerpt: These recommended security levels reflect our current thinking proportionate to the risks posed and may be adjusted if our understanding of the risks changes.
paraphrase: The recommended security levels reflect current thinking proportionate to risk and may be adjusted as understanding changes.

excerpt: This may occur if, for example, a model does not possess capabilities meaningfully different from other publicly available models that have weaker security applied (in which case the marginal benefit of higher security is limited), or if we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
paraphrase: Adjustment may occur if a model's capabilities are not meaningfully different from weaker-secured public models, or if open release benefits are judged to outweigh risks.

excerpt: Relatedly, we believe these recommendations will only be effective if the entire frontier AI field applies them, and of limited social utility if not.
paraphrase: These recommendations are believed effective only with field-wide adoption, and of limited social value otherwise.

excerpt: This risk domain focuses on risks of models assisting in the development, preparation and/or execution of a CBRN threat.
paraphrase: The CBRN domain covers risks of models assisting in developing, preparing, or executing CBRN threats.
